title: Bring Back Chivalry: A Reply to Aaron Renn
author: Dr. Leonard Sax
summary: Leonard Sax replies to Aaron Renn's IFS essay on why young men are drawn to the manosphere. Renn had criticized Sax by name for urging boys to be gentlemen and advised avoiding appeals to retro concepts and norms. Sax answers that Renn cites pollster Daniel Cox approvingly while apparently overlooking Cox's new book, Generation Uncoupled, which ends with a call to return to chivalry as a model of masculinity that benefited society. He points to the Boys to Men program, which draws on traditional values and reports an 85 percent drop in school discipline referrals over thirty years, and quotes C. S. Lewis on turning back when one is on the wrong road. Sax adds that Renn's essay is largely negative and offers only vague suggestions, whereas his own decades as a family physician convince him that boys need a positive model to work toward. His conclusion is that popular culture offers few role models, so young men must be given something to aspire to.

quotes: Interestingly, Renn cites the work of pollster Daniel Cox at some length—with approval. But he appears not to have read Cox’s excellent new book, Generation Uncoupled
At the end of the book, Cox calls for a return to chivalry, “not to diminish women, but to recover a model of masculinity that benefited society.

When I have spoken with co-founders Craig McClain and Joe Sigurdson, they do not hesitate to appeal to traditional values and norms to inspire boys. And they now have 30 years of data showing the effectiveness of their program: boys who participate experience an 85% drop in school discipline referrals.
If you are on the wrong road, progress means doing an about-turn and walking back to the right road; and in that case the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man.
Renn’s essay is largely negative, explaining what he didn’t like about my post for IFS, or about Chris Hatch’s viral social media post
We must provide a positive model that boys can understand and work toward. And that may require “appeals to retro concepts and norms,” like learning how to be gentleman.
Current American popular culture offers few good role models, so we have to give young men something to aspire to. Which is why I agree with Cox: Bring back chivalry.
